How much to charge to install quartz countertops

The number a homeowner wants is a price per finished square foot. That number is not a takeoff. A 40 sq ft galley with a drop-in sink is not the same job as a 28 sq ft island with two waterfall ends. The footage is smaller on the island. The slabs are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count slabs and cutouts, not just finished footage

A typical quartz slab is about 46 usable square feet. Layout waste — corners, seams, and the leftover after you pull an L — turns that into fewer finished feet than the homeowner measured. Flooring install prices waste and tear-out of planks. Cabinet refinishing prices doors and drawers. Stone fabrication prices whole slabs plus every polished hole. Quoting both from a published per-square-foot number is how the second slab eats the field margin.

Waterfalls are extra stone, not a blended add-on

Each waterfall end is typically 36 inches high by about 25.5 inches deep — a little over six square feet that never appears in the island-top measurement — plus the hours to miter, polish, and set it. On the sample rates a 28 sq ft island with two waterfall ends needs two slabs and prices about $4,597 ($164 per finished square foot). The same shop’s 40 sq ft galley with a drop-in and an eased edge fits one slab at about $2,383 ($60 per finished square foot). Matching the galley’s per-square-foot number on the island is how that job becomes a loss.

Undermount holes and ogee edges do not scale with the top

A drop-in sink is a cut. An undermount is a cut plus a polished hole. A cooktop is another hole. Ogee, bullnose, and mitered laminated edges are lineal-foot labor on the finished perimeter. A default 55 sq ft L-kitchen with an undermount, a cooktop, 18 feet of 4-inch splash, and ogee edges prices about $5,119 on the sample rates ($93 per finished square foot, 24.9 crew-hours, two slabs, walk-away $3,839). Edges and the splash take more hours than the field cut. Treating that as a blended “add 20%” is how the L-kitchen special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first seam.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h fabricator loaded at 30% payroll burden is $49.40. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a stone specification, a color or lot match, a seam or lead-time warranty, a permit, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Slab yield, sink model, and whether the waterfall is mitered or laminated are yours to confirm.

Price your kitchen

Common questions

How much to charge to install quartz countertops?

Charge from finished square footage, layout waste into whole slabs, sink and cooktop cutouts, edge profile, backsplash, waterfall ends, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 55 sq ft L-kitchen with an undermount, a cooktop, and ogee edges prices around $5,119 on the sample rates in this calculator — about $93 per finished square foot.

Why is a per-square-foot quartz quote dangerous?

Homeowners measure finished tops. Slabs, polished holes, mitered edges, and waterfall ends do not scale with that footage. Matching a cheaper per-square-foot quote written for a straight galley is how a waterfall island becomes a two-slab loss.

How many slabs do I need for a small waterfall island?

Treat each waterfall as extra stone — typically 36 inches high by about 25.5 inches deep, plus layout waste — not a blended add-on to the island top. On the sample rates a 28 sq ft island with two waterfall ends needs two 46 sq ft slabs and prices around $4,597 ($164 per finished square foot), while a larger 40 sq ft galley with no splash fits one slab at about $2,383.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours, waste, and slab sizes are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a color match, or a stone specification — replace them with your own template.

      Common questions

      Why does a 28 sq ft waterfall island cost more per foot than a 55 sq ft L-kitchen?

      Because waterfall ends consume whole extra slab, not extra finished square footage. Each waterfall end wraps the countertop down the side of the island in one continuous piece, so it is billed and fabricated by the slab, not by the sq ft rate. A small island with two waterfalls can use more stone — and more shop hours — than a much larger straight run with none. That is the “slab trap” preset: 28 sq ft, no sink, no cooktop, still one of the pricier jobs on the list.

      Why does layout change the price for the same finished square footage?

      Because waste percent scales with how many cuts and returns the layout needs, not with the visible countertop area. A straight galley run starts at 12% waste. An L-shape starts at 20%. A U-shape starts at 28%, and a run with an island starts at 24%. Two kitchens with identical finished square footage can need very different amounts of slab once the layout’s starting waste percent is applied.

      What is the real cost difference between an eased edge and a mitered edge?

      About 5.6× the labor per linear foot. An eased or pencil edge starts at 0.08 hours per linear foot. A bevel starts at 0.12. An ogee or bullnose starts at 0.22. A mitered, laminated edge — the thick-look edge on an island — starts at 0.45 hours per linear foot, because it is built up from a second strip of stone glued and finished to look solid. The edge profile you pick refills the starting hours automatically so the swing shows up before you touch a rate.

      Why does an undermount sink cost more than a drop-in for the same cutout?

      A drop-in sink sits on top of the counter, so the cutout edge is hidden under the sink’s own rim — roughly 0.6 hours. An undermount sink hangs below the stone, so the cut edge is fully visible and has to be polished, which starts at 2 hours. A farmhouse or apron-front sink needs the counter itself notched to fit around the front of the sink and starts at 3 hours. Same hole in the counter, very different finishing work.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your dimensions, wages, or prices. Only your business details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser’s local storage so you do not retype them, and the customer’s details are never saved.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — template and fabrication hours, slabs, sink and cooktop cutouts, edges, backsplash, and waterfalls — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Quartz & Granite Countertop Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per finished square foot

"$60 a finished square foot, installed" is not a price for a countertop — it is a price for one plain galley run with a drop-in sink, quietly applied to an island with an undermount sink, an ogee edge, and two waterfall ends.

What a flat price-per-square-foot quote is

A flat per-square-foot number is the fastest way to bid over the phone or match a homeowner's forum post: one figure, easy to multiply by any finished footage, and the number a caller holding a competitor's estimate will ask you to match on their own kitchen.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually a plain, easy galley run with a drop-in sink, an eased edge, and no waterfalls — and then reused for every kitchen afterward, whether or not the next job has an undermount or farmhouse sink to polish, a mitered edge, two waterfall ends wrapping an island, or a U-shape layout that eats far more slab than the same footage in a straight run.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter finished square footage, layout, material, sink and cooktop cutouts, edge profile, backsplash, waterfall ends, and your own shop rates. It prices slab count from layout waste, cutout and edge labor, and waterfall ends separately, and returns a walk-away price and price per finished square foot below which the job loses money — for this kitchen, not a generic one.

Job$60/sq ft quoteWalk-away priceVerdict
40 sq ft galley, drop-in sink, eased edge, no waterfalls$2,400.00$1,787.55Covers, $612.45 to spare
55 sq ft L-kitchen, undermount sink + cooktop, ogee edge (this calculator's own default job)$3,300.00$3,839.07Short $539.07
28 sq ft island, no sink, two waterfall ends, mitered edge (the slab trap)$1,680.00$3,447.95Short $1,767.95

Worked using this calculator's own job presets at a $38 hourly wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, and a 25% target margin — the form's own shipped defaults, not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator to check any row yourself.

Notice the middle row: it is this calculator's own shipped starting point, not a job picked to prove a point, and a $60/sq ft quote already falls over five hundred dollars short of it. The bottom row is the sharper case -- 28 sq ft is a small kitchen by any flat-rate math, yet two waterfall ends consume enough extra slab and labor to make it the most expensive job on the list. A flat square-foot number cannot see a waterfall at all, because a waterfall end is not finished top.

What a flat price-per-square-foot quote doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate whether the layout is a straight galley run or a U-shape with an island — applying the same waste percent to both. Applies layout waste by shape (12% galley up to 28% U-shape) before converting required stone into whole slabs, so an L-shape or U-shape prices differently from a straight run.
Has no separate line for a sink or cooktop cutout, so a drop-in, an undermount, and a farmhouse hole are absorbed into the same per-square-foot number. Prices sink and cooktop cutout labor separately, scaled to how much finishing the hole actually needs — a drop-in hides the cut edge under its own rim; an undermount or farmhouse sink leaves it fully exposed and polished.
Prices a waterfall end the same as ordinary finished square footage, or has no line for it at all. Adds a waterfall end's own slab area and its own labor hours, since a waterfall wraps the countertop down the side of an island in one continuous piece rather than adding finished top the homeowner measures.
Charges one edge rate no matter the profile, though a mitered edge runs roughly 5.6× the labor of an eased edge per lineal foot. Prices edge labor per lineal foot by the profile actually chosen — eased, bevel, ogee, or mitered.
Gives the homeowner a price to shop, not a number to check a quote against once the kitchen turns out to have an undermount sink and two waterfall ends after the flat rate was already promised. Reports the walk-away price and price per finished square foot for the job as entered, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before it is confirmed.

A flat price-per-square-foot quote is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a layout, sink, edge profile, or waterfall count it was not set on, and "a countertop" alone never tells you that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price-per-finished-square-foot countertop quote get the price wrong?

Because countertop cost scales with layout waste, sink and cooktop cutouts, edge profile, seams, and waterfall ends — not with finished square footage alone. A straight galley run with a drop-in sink and an eased edge is a different job from the same footage in an island with an undermount sink, an ogee edge, and two waterfall ends. A flat per-square-foot price quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat price-per-square-foot quote usually leave out entirely?

Layout waste that turns finished footage into whole slabs, sink and cooktop cutout labor, the edge profile actually chosen, seams, and waterfall ends — which consume a whole extra slab wrapped down the side of an island rather than adding finished top. A published per-square-foot number is set on one configuration — usually a plain galley run with a drop-in sink and an eased edge — and has no separate line for any of those.

How much do sink cutouts, edge profile, and waterfall ends actually add over a flat rate?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $38 hourly wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, and a 25% target margin: a 40 sq ft galley with a drop-in sink and an eased edge walks away at $1,787.55, comfortably under a $60/sq ft, $2,400.00 quote. This calculator's own shipped default job — a 55 sq ft L-kitchen with an undermount sink, a cooktop cutout, and an ogee edge — walks away at $3,839.07, $539.07 short of that same $60/sq ft number. A 28 sq ft island with two waterfall ends and no sink at all — the calculator's own "slab trap" preset — walks away at $3,447.95, $1,767.95 short of a $60/sq ft, $1,680.00 quote.

Is a flat price-per-square-foot quote ever the right way to bid a countertop job?

For something close to the easy run it was probably priced on — a straight galley, a drop-in sink, an eased edge, no waterfalls — a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own numbers that easy job clears a $60/sq ft quote with over $600 to spare. The risk is an undermount or farmhouse sink, a mitered edge, and waterfall ends stacking on top of each other, because a flat per-square-foot price has no way to see any of them until the slab is already on the truck.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local slab costs or what competitors charge. It takes the finished footage, layout, cutouts, edge profile, and waterfall ends you enter, plus your own wage, burden, and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot number skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat price per finished square foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the layout, sink, edge, and waterfall count it was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

← Quartz & Granite Countertop Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Moraware CounterGo

Two different shapes: CounterGo is an account-based platform for drawing, quoting, and cut-listing a stone shop's jobs across its whole production floor. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this job cost, before you draw it or quote it.

What each tool is for

Moraware CounterGo is drawing, quoting, and cut-layout software built specifically for countertop and stone fabrication shops, from single-shop operators to multi-location fabricators. Shops use it to draw a room's actual counter layout, generate a customer-facing quote from that drawing, and lay finished pieces out on slabs so the shop floor knows what to cut. Moraware sells CounterGo on an ongoing, account-based subscription and also offers a separate product, Systemize, for tracking a job through templating, fabrication, and installation, which shops commonly run alongside it. Moraware's own site does not publish specific plan names or dollar pricing, so no figure for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category are stated, and no dollar amount for CounterGo appears on this page. Public descriptions of that software describe drawing a room and laying cut pieces out on slabs the shop has already bought; none describe estimating, from a rough takeoff of finished square footage, cutouts, edges, and waterfalls alone, what the whole job should sell for before a drawing exists — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what CounterGo does. It does not draw a room, store a customer record, or lay finished pieces out on a specific slab for the saw. It takes one job's finished square footage, its layout shape (straight, L, U, or island) and the waste percent that shape implies, sink and cooktop cutout hours by mount type, edge profile, backsplash length, and waterfall ends, plus fabricator wage, payroll burden, and target margin, and turns that into the slabs the takeoff actually consumes, the price per finished square foot, the bid price, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to draw a room's actual layout, quote from that drawing, and lay finished pieces out on slabs for my shop floor.CounterGo, or a comparable stone-shop platform — drawing and cut-layout is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this job, given its footage, layout shape, cutouts, edges, and waterfalls, before I open a drawing tool?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How many slabs does a small waterfall island really consume next to a bigger galley with no splash?This calculator's slab count from layout waste and waterfall stone, not a blended per-square-foot guess.
Is the price I'm about to send still above my walk-away cost?This calculator's compare-to-proposed-price check.
I already draw every room and need one system tracking quotes, templates, and slab layout through production, across many jobs.CounterGo (often paired with Moraware's Systemize) — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a per-job countertop price actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. CounterGo is used through a paid account.

Most stone fabrication shops get different value from each: CounterGo (or a comparable stone-shop platform) for drawing every room, quoting from that drawing, and running templates and slab layout through production as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what a job should cost from a rough takeoff before a drawing exists. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal, an invoice, or a fabrication guarantee.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Moraware CounterGo?

They do different jobs, and a stone fabrication shop of any size will likely end up touching both. Moraware CounterGo is drawing, quoting, and cut-layout software used by countertop and stone fabrication shops, sold on an ongoing per-user account basis, often alongside Moraware's separate Systemize product for tracking a job through production. It is built to draw a room's actual layout, generate a customer quote from that drawing, and lay the pieces out on slabs for the shop floor. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from finished square footage, layout waste by shape, sink and cooktop cutouts, edge profile, backsplash, and waterfall ends, it turns that into the price per finished square foot, the whole slabs the takeoff actually consumes, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before you have quoted or drawn anything. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A shop that already draws every room and needs one system tracking quotes, templates, and slab layout through production is better served by CounterGo or a comparable stone-shop platform; a fabricator who wants an instant, private gut-check on what a job should cost from a rough takeoff, before opening a drawing tool, is in the right place here.
